intro: The single most-sung wedding verse in Hebrew, and the reason it works is the sentence it is lifted out of. Jeremiah is describing a ruin: a place with no people and no animals, empty streets, a city everyone has written off. Then the same sentence keeps going and says that in that exact place there will be heard the voice of joy, the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride. The wedding song is the back half of a sentence about a wasteland, and singing it without knowing that loses most of it.

stanzas.label: the ruin

stichs.en: Thus says the LORD: yet again shall be heard in this place
of which you say: it is a ruin, with no man and no beast,
in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem that are desolate, with no man and no inhabitant and no beast:

stanzas.summary: This stanza is never sung and it is the reason the next one means anything. Note {{0.12}}, {{0.14}}, {{0.21}}, {{0.23}} and {{0.25}}: the same word for "with none of" five times in two verses. Hebrew is not short of ways to say empty; it chose to say the same thing five times, which is what emptiness sounds like.

stanzas.label: the voices

stichs.en: the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride,
the voice of those who say: give thanks to the LORD of hosts, for the LORD is good, for His mercy endures for ever,
as they bring thanksgiving to the house of the LORD.
For I will restore the fortunes of the land as at the first, says the LORD.

stanzas.summary: The wedding song is the first stich alone: five occurrences of {{1.0}} and its paired form {{1.2}}, four of them naming a sound that was absent from the ruin. The pairing of {{1.5}} and {{1.7}} is the line everyone knows, and it is the fourth item in a list, not the subject of the verse. What is being promised is noise in an empty street.

chantTips: The sung portion is the first stich of the second stanza, repeated until the dancing stops. Everything else on this page is context.
It is a dance tune. Once the circle is moving, the tempo goes where the circle takes it and the guitar follows.
Two phrases, then two phrases: {{1.1}} and {{1.3}} answer each other, then {{1.5}} and {{1.7}} do. Sing it as four short arcs, not one long line.
There are many melodies for this verse and they are all in current use. Ask which one before you start playing, or start singing and let the room correct you.

about.body: Jeremiah 33:10-11. Jeremiah 33 is written from a siege — the prophet is under guard and the city is about to fall — and the chapter is a series of promises made at the worst possible moment. This is one of them.

From {{1.10}} to {{1.19}} the verse quotes the Temple thanksgiving formula, which appears word for word in several psalms. Jeremiah is not composing that line; he is predicting that people will be heard saying it again. The wedding song therefore contains a psalm inside a prophecy inside a wedding.

The bridegroom and the bride appear in this verse as a measure of whether a place is alive. A wedding is the moment the community can point at the verse and say it has come true, which is why it is sung at that moment and not, for instance, at a memorial.
